description:
Start with a real project

Write down the query, the page that should answer it and the information a reader needs next.

Review the first version

Review the draft against the page's purpose. Replace broad advice with a concrete example and keep language that sounds natural when read aloud.

Check the final result

Check facts and citations before publishing. Use Search Console to track page-level results when you have verified query data.

Frequently asked questions

Will adding more keywords improve a page?

Use terms that help you answer the reader's question. Look at page relevance and clarity alongside query performance.

Browse related tools on SEOGBTools.

Choose the page and the search question

Start with one article or product page that has a clear job. Write down what the reader should know after visiting it. A product page for a compact desk lamp could help someone check whether the lamp fits beside a monitor. A guide could answer how to reduce glare while working. The two pages can link to each other because they answer different questions.

Look at public search results for the main question and a few related phrases. Note which results explain the topic well and what they leave unanswered. For the lamp example, several pages may talk about glare while giving few examples of where to place the light. A diagram and two practical setups would give the reader something to try.

Give the first draft real material

Supply the product dimensions, the steps you tested, and any conditions the writer should preserve. Ask for headings that match the reader's decisions. Review the outline before writing the full draft. Move the clearest answer near the top, then use the rest of the article to show examples and explain exceptions.

AISEO documents a paraphraser with options that change the style or length of a passage. Pick a short section to revise first. Compare it with the source and check names, dates, quantities, and the conditions attached to each claim. If a sentence starts to promise more than the source supports, restore the original meaning in clearer words.

Review the page before publishing

Read the draft on a phone. Look for sentences that take several lines, headings that repeat each other, and links that interrupt a step. Place links where they give readers a next action. A paragraph about collecting keyword ideas can point to KeywordTool.io. A section about reviewing ranking changes can point to SE Ranking.

Record the page URL and the questions the revision covers. Use Search Console data when available to compare clicks and impressions for that specific page. Keep public keyword suggestions labeled in your editorial notes. Search results can help you choose a topic, while Search Console measures the queries that actually reached your site.

Check the current SEOGBTools offer if you need a specific AISEO feature, usage limit, or language. Use a public or sample passage for your first test, then review the time you spent drafting and checking the result.

Turn a search question into a practical outline

Suppose you run a shop that sells desk lamps and want to improve a guide about glare. Read the current page and mark the point where a visitor can try the first fix. If the answer only appears after several paragraphs, move it higher. A short opening can explain how to angle the lamp away from the screen and check the reflection from the usual sitting position.

Build the rest of the outline around the cases the opening does not cover. Add a section for desks next to windows and another for people who use more than one monitor. Describe what to check in each setup and where to place the lamp. Include a photo or diagram only when it shows the position more clearly than a paragraph can.

Give the drafting tool the real measurements and observations you have. If the page describes a lamp with a short arm, use the size from the product specifications. If a setup has only been tested with one monitor, keep that detail visible in the draft. Clear evidence gives an editor a way to check the paragraph before it goes public.

Check what the rewrite changed

Read the original and revised versions side by side. Mark changes to the promise, the conditions, and the order of instructions. A sentence can sound clearer while making the underlying claim stronger. For instance, saying a different lamp position can reduce glare is narrower than saying it will remove glare in every room. Keep the language within what the example supports.

Look for paragraphs that use the same idea in different words. Keep the example that serves the heading and move any useful detail into it. Then check that a reader can move from one section to the next without having to remember a term you introduced much earlier. A short reminder can be useful when a page is long and people may jump to a section from search.

Where should related keywords appear?

Use the wording readers recognize in the heading or sentence that answers their question. A heading about screen glare should lead to a practical answer about reflections or light placement. Keep other search terms in your research notes when the page has no useful answer for them.
